claim: The integrated stress response (ISR) is activated by diverse forms of cellular stress, including endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress.
source: The integrated stress response (ISR) is activated by diverse forms of cellular stress, including endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, and is associated with diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to established literature on the ISR.

claim: The protein kinase RNA-like ER kinase (PERK) pathway mediates preferential synthesis of ATF4 and CHOP.
source: We show the protein kinase RNA-like ER kinase (PERK) pathway that mediates preferential synthesis of ATF4 and CHOP, dominates in causing dysplasia by reverting chondrocyte differentiation via ATF4-directed transactivation of Sox9.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PERK pathway dominates in causing dysplasia by reverting chondrocyte differentiation via ATF4-directed transactivation of Sox9.
source: We show the protein kinase RNA-like ER kinase (PERK) pathway that mediates preferential synthesis of ATF4 and CHOP, dominates in causing dysplasia by reverting chondrocyte differentiation via ATF4-directed transactivation of Sox9.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by genetic and molecular data in the manuscript.

claim: Chondrocyte survival is enabled cell autonomously by CHOP and dual CHOP-ATF4 transactivation of Fgf21.
source: Chondrocyte survival is enabled, cell autonomously, by CHOP and dual CHOP-ATF4 transactivation of Fgf21.
evidence: This is supported by chimera experiments and molecular analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Treatment of mutant mice with a chemical inhibitor of PERK signaling prevents the differentiation defects and ameliorates chondrodysplasia.
source: Treatment of mutant mice with a chemical inhibitor of PERK signaling prevents the differentiation defects and ameliorates chondrodysplasia.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ISRIB treatment experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: The ISR can be stimulated by hypoxia, amino acid deprivation, glucose/nutrition deprivation, and viral infection.
source: The ISR can be stimulated by a range of physiological or pathological changes (Brostrom et al., 1996; Dever et al., 1992; Harding et al., 2003; Ron, 2002; Wek et al., 2006), including hypoxia, amino acid deprivation, glucose/nutrition deprivation, viral infection (Dever et al., 1992; Harding et al., 2003; Wek et al., 2006; García et al., 2007; Rzymski et al., 2010; Ye et al., 2010) and intrinsic endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (Harding et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Intrinsic ER stress is caused by the accumulation of unfolded or misfolded proteins within ER.
source: intrinsic endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (Harding et al., 1999), which is caused by the accumulation of unfolded or misfolded proteins within ER.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citation.

claim: Oncogene activation can trigger the ISR in the context of cancer biology.
source: Furthermore, in the context of cancer biology, oncogene activation can also trigger the ISR (Denoyelle et al., 2006; Hart et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The ISR is primarily a pro-survival homeostatic program aiming to optimize the adaptive cellular response to stress.
source: Although the ISR is primarily a pro-survival homeostatic program, aiming to optimize the adaptive cellular response to stress, exposure to severe stress, either in intensity or duration, will overwhelm the capacity of this adaptive response and drive signaling toward cell death.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Severe or prolonged stress can overwhelm the ISR adaptive response and drive signaling toward cell death.
source: Although the ISR is primarily a pro-survival homeostatic program, aiming to optimize the adaptive cellular response to stress, exposure to severe stress, either in intensity or duration, will overwhelm the capacity of this adaptive response and drive signaling toward cell death.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The key early controlling step in the ISR is the phosphorylation of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 alpha (eIF2α).
source: The key early controlling step in the ISR is the phosphorylation of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 alpha (eIF2α) by one of four members of eIF2α kinase family: protein kinase R (PKR), PKR-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK), general control nonderepressible 2 (GCN2), and Heme-regulated eIF2α kinase (HRI) (Dever et al., 1992; García et al., 2007; Harding et al., 1999; Han et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Four members of the eIF2α kinase family are PKR, PERK, GCN2, and HRI.
source: The key early controlling step in the ISR is the phosphorylation of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 alpha (eIF2α) by one of four members of eIF2α kinase family: protein kinase R (PKR), PKR-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK), general control nonderepressible 2 (GCN2), and Heme-regulated eIF2α kinase (HRI) (Dever et al., 1992; García et al., 2007; Harding et al., 1999; Han et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: eIF2α kinases phosphorylate serine 51 in eIF2α.
source: These kinases phosphorylate serine 51 in eIF2α, promoting the formation of a p-eIF2α and eIF2B complex, consequently inhibiting the guanine nucleotide exchange activity of eIF2B (Sudhakar et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α promotes the formation of a p-eIF2α and eIF2B complex.
source: These kinases phosphorylate serine 51 in eIF2α, promoting the formation of a p-eIF2α and eIF2B complex, consequently inhibiting the guanine nucleotide exchange activity of eIF2B (Sudhakar et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Formation of p-eIF2α and eIF2B complex inhibits the guanine nucleotide exchange activity of eIF2B.
source: These kinases phosphorylate serine 51 in eIF2α, promoting the formation of a p-eIF2α and eIF2B complex, consequently inhibiting the guanine nucleotide exchange activity of eIF2B (Sudhakar et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Inactivation of the eIF2 complex leads to a shutdown of global protein synthesis.
source: Inactivation of the eIF2 complex leads to a shutdown of global protein synthesis but also the induction of preferential translation of transcripts notably the mRNAs of transcription factors, Activating Transcription Factor 4 (ATF4) and C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP, encoded by Ddit3), and other factors with both pro-survival and pro-death functions which aid cell adaption and recovery (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (Harding et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and referenced figure.

claim: Inactivation of the eIF2 complex induces preferential translation of ATF4 and CHOP mRNAs.
source: Inactivation of the eIF2 complex leads to a shutdown of global protein synthesis but also the induction of preferential translation of transcripts notably the mRNAs of transcription factors, Activating Transcription Factor 4 (ATF4) and C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP, encoded by Ddit3), and other factors with both pro-survival and pro-death functions which aid cell adaption and recovery (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (Harding et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CHOP is encoded by Ddit3.
source: Inactivation of the eIF2 complex leads to a shutdown of global protein synthesis but also the induction of preferential translation of transcripts notably the mRNAs of transcription factors, Activating Transcription Factor 4 (ATF4) and C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP, encoded by Ddit3), and other factors with both pro-survival and pro-death functions which aid cell adaption and recovery (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (Harding et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation is transient and can be reversed by PPP1R15A (GADD34) or CReP1.
source: eIF2α phosphorylation is transient and can be reversed by PPP1R15A (GADD34) or CReP1, the regulatory subunit of eIF2α phosphatases, acting in a negative feedback loop that allows protein synthesis to restart (Harding et al., 2009; Novoa et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PPP1R15A and CReP1 act in a negative feedback loop that allows protein synthesis to restart.
source: eIF2α phosphorylation is transient and can be reversed by PPP1R15A (GADD34) or CReP1, the regulatory subunit of eIF2α phosphatases, acting in a negative feedback loop that allows protein synthesis to restart (Harding et al., 2009; Novoa et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: When stress is intense or prolonged, cells fail to adapt and apoptosis is triggered.
source: When the stress is intense or prolonged, cells fail to adapt, and apoptosis is triggered.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The duration and level of eIF2α phosphorylation, as well as ATF4 regulation, determine the balance between cell survival and cell death.
source: It is likely that the duration and level of eIF2α phosphorylation, as well as ATF4 regulation, determine the balance between cell survival and cell death.
evidence: This is an inference based on the established knowledge presented.

claim: There are more than 400 human genetic skeletal disorders caused by disrupted cartilage and bone development and growth.
source: There are more than 400 human genetic skeletal disorders caused by disrupted cartilage and bone development and growth, commonly resulting in dwarfism and skeletal deformities (Geister and Camper, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Many skeletal disorders are caused by mutations in genes for extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins.
source: Many of these disorders are caused by mutations in genes for extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins (Geister and Camper, 2015; Bonafe et al., 2015; Briggs and Chapman, 2002; Warman et al., 1993)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Some mutations in ECM protein genes cause inappropriate folding, processing or export, leading to retention in the ER.
source: and some mutations cause inappropriate folding, processing or export, leading to retention in the ER, affecting the secretory and stress response pathways (Wilson et al., 2005; Tsang et al., 2007; Tsang et al., 2010; Posey et al., 2012; PirogPiróg-Garcia et al., 2007; Hartley et al., 2013; Cameron et al., 2011; Boot-Handford and Briggs, 2010; Arnold and Fertala, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER can overwhelm the protein quality control mechanism, causing proteotoxicity, cell cycle arrest and cell death.
source: Accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER can overwhelm the protein quality control mechanism, causing proteotoxicity, cell cycle arrest and cell death.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cells activate the unfolded protein response (UPR) which mediates cell survival by slowing protein translation, promoting proteostasis via the proteasome and activating transcription factors that upregulate the production of protein chaperones.
source: Cells activate the unfolded protein response (UPR), which mediates cell survival by slowing protein translation, promoting proteostasis via the proteasome and activating transcription factors that upregulate the production of protein chaperones (reviewed in [Hotamisligil and Davis, 2016; Horiuchi et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The UPR employs three arms of sensors in the ER: PERK, IRE1α, and the ATF6 family.
source: The UPR employs three arms of sensors in the ER to mediate cell adaptation and survival under ER stress: the key component of the ISR, PERK, inositol-regulated enzyme 1α (IRE1α), and the activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6) family (Hotamisligil and Davis, 2016; Horiuchi et al., 2016; Walter and Ron, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Upon ER stress, the PERK-p-eIF2α signaling modulates cell adaptation via translational control.
source: Upon ER stress, the PERK-p-eIF2α signaling modulates the cell adaptation via translational control.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: ATF6 family factors move from the ER to the Golgi, are processed by S1 and S2 proteases, and translocate to the nucleus to activate ER quality control genes such as Hspa5 and Xbp1.
source: ATF6 family factors move from the ER to the Golgi, are processed by S1 and S2 proteases, and translocate to the nucleus to activate ER quality control genes such as Hspa5 (encodes BiP) and Xbp1 (X-box binding protein 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: IRE1α has kinase and endoribonuclease (RNase) activities.
source: IRE1α has kinase and endoribonuclease (RNase) activities.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: IRE1α catalyzes the splicing of Xbp1 mRNA, generating the UPR transcription factor XBP1S.
source: It catalyzes the splicing of Xbp1 mRNA, generating the UPR transcription factor XBP1S that upregulates genes encoding chaperones and proteins involved in ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: XBP1S upregulates genes encoding chaperones and proteins involved in ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD).
source: It catalyzes the splicing of Xbp1 mRNA, generating the UPR transcription factor XBP1S that upregulates genes encoding chaperones and proteins involved in ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: In the MCDS transgenic mouse model (13del), misfolded mutant collagen X induces ER stress.
source: In an MCDS transgenic mouse model (13del), carrying a 13 bp deletion in Col10a1 equivalent to the human mutation, misfolded mutant collagen X induces ER stress suggesting the primary role of ER stress in MCDS pathogenesis (Tsang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In 13del mice, chondrocyte differentiation is reversed to a more juvenile state characterized by re-expression of prehypertrophic chondrocyte markers.
source: Although the chondrocytes survive, their differentiation is reversed by an unknown mechanism to a more juvenile state characterized by the re-expression of prehypertrophic chondrocyte markers (Ppr, Sox9 and Col2a1), disrupting endochondral ossification, and skeletal dysplasia ensues.
evidence: This is a finding from previous work on the 13del model.

claim: Expression of an exogenous misfolded protein in HCs can induce an MCDS-like phenotype.
source: The causative role of ER stress in MCDS is further supported by studies showing that expression of an exogenous misfolded protein in HCs can induce an MCDS-like phenotype (Rajpar et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Skeletal defects caused by mutations that induce stress or inactivate critical transducers of the stress response in humans and mouse models implicate components of ER stress-induced UPR pathways in chondrocyte and osteoblast differentiation.
source: It is noteworthy that the skeletal defects caused by mutations that induce stress or inactivate critical transducers of the stress response in humans (Julier and Nicolino, 2010) and mouse models (Tsang et al., 2007; Cameron et al., 2011; Horiuchi et al., 2016; Rajpar et al., 2009; Julier and Nicolino, 2010; Nundlall et al., 2010; Cameron et al., 2015a2015; Cameron et al., 2015b) strongly implicate components of ER stress-induced UPR pathways involved in chondrocyte and osteoblast differentiation (Tsang et al., 2010; Horiuchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Expression of misfolded cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) in proliferating and hypertrophic chondrocytes results in chondrocyte disorganization and causes Pseudoachondroplasia (PSACH).
source: Expression of misfolded cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) in proliferating and hypertrophic chondrocytes results in chondrocyte disorganization and causes Pseudoachondroplasia (PSACH), suggesting triggering the UPR may underlie many chondrodysplasias where mutations cause accumulation of misfolded proteins (Posey et al., 2012; Piróg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Bbf2h7 null mutants show severe chondrocyte abnormality due to proliferation and differentiation defects.
source: Another example that links ER stress signaling to chondrocyte differentiation is illustrated by studies on BBF2H7, an ER stress transducer. Bbf2h7 null mutants show severe chondrocyte abnormality due to proliferation and differentiation defects, indicating its essential role for chondrogenesis (Saito et al., 2009; Saito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: BBF2H7 suppresses chondrocyte hypertrophy by direct regulation of IHH signaling and the IHH-PTHrP pathway.
source: Furthermore, BBF2H7 has been shown to suppress chondrocyte hypertrophy by direct regulation of IHH signaling and the IHH-PTHrP pathway (Saito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Pharmacological stimulation of intracellular proteolysis of mutant collagen X in an MCDS mouse model reduces the level of ER stress and partially ameliorates the dwarfism phenotype.
source: Pharmacological stimulation of intracellular proteolysis of mutant collagen X in another MCDS mouse model reduces the level of ER stress, partially ameliorating the dwarfism phenotype (Mullan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Stimulating degradation of misfolded protein alone is not sufficient to address the impact of ER stress on aberrant cell differentiation in MCDS.
source: However, the rescue of the chondrocyte differentiation defect, expansion of the hypertrophic zone and bone growth was incomplete, suggesting stimulating degradation of misfolded protein alone is not sufficient to address the impact of the ER stress on aberrant cell differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the incomplete rescue observed in the cited study.

claim: The mammalian growth plate comprises four major sub-populations of chondrocytes: resting, proliferating (PC), prehypertrophic (pHC) and hypertrophic chondrocytes (HC).
source: The mammalian growth plate comprises four major sub-populations of chondrocytes: resting, proliferating (PC), prehypertrophic (pHC) and hypertrophic chondrocytes (HC).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Chondrocytes in the growth plate have distinct morphologies and gene expression profiles governed by a precisely tuned gene regulatory network.
source: These chondrocytes have distinct morphologies and gene expression profiles governed by a precisely tuned gene regulatory network (Hojo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Proximal tibial growth plates from 10-day-old WT and 13del mice were fractionated into sub-populations representing proliferating (PZ), prehypertrophic (pHZ) and hypertrophic chondrocytes (HZ).
source: To investigate the effect of ER stress on the transcriptome of HCs, the proximal tibial growth plates from 10-day-old WT and 13del mice were fractionated into sub-populations representing proliferating (PZ), prehypertrophic (pHZ) and hypertrophic chondrocytes (HZ) (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The wild-type HZ was fractionated into upper and lower zones (UHZ and LHZ) to capture early onset and late phases of hypertrophy.
source: The wild-type HZ was fractionated into upper and lower zones (UHZ and LHZ) to capture early onset and late phases of hypertrophy.
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: The 13del HZ was fractionated into three zones: upper (UHZ), middle (MHZ), and lower (LHZ).
source: The 13del HZ was fractionated into three zones: upper (UHZ) corresponding to the early phase of UPR activation, middle (MHZ) where HC adaptation would be initiated, and lower (LHZ) where HC should fully adapt.
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: K-means clustering categorized gene expression patterns across different zones in wild-type and 13del growth plates into four clusters.
source: We used k-means clustering (see Materials and methods) to categorize the gene expression patterns across different zones in wild-type and 13del growth plates into four clusters (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a methodological description and analysis result.

claim: Cluster I contains 453 genes that increased expression from PHZ to lower HZ specifically in 13del HC.
source: Genes (453) in Cluster I increased expression from PHZ to lower HZ specifically in 13del HC (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1B and C showing the clustering analysis.

claim: Cluster I genes are mainly involved in protein processing in the ER and the UPR.
source: Ontological analyses show these differentially expressed genes are mainly involved in protein processing in the ER and the UPR (Figure 1D and E, Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by ontological analyses shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Cluster II contains 659 genes and Cluster III contains 314 genes that showed highest expression in wild-type PZ and pHZ followed by progressive downregulation from pHZ to LHZ but were upregulated in 13del LHZ.
source: Genes in Clusters II (659) and III (314) showed highest expression in wild-type PZ and pHZ followed by progressive downregulation from pHZ to LHZ but were upregulated in 13del LHZ, reflecting UPR-induced changes in HC differentiation (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1B and C showing the clustering analysis.

claim: Cluster II and III genes include Sox9, Ppr, and Ihh.
source: These genes included Sox9, Ppr, and Ihh, consistent with our previous report of re-expression of pre-hypertrophic markers (Tsang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis and previous work.

claim: Cluster IV contains 680 genes showing increasing expression from pHZ to LHZ in wild-type and can be defined as 'hypertrophy characteristic' genes.
source: Cluster IV genes (680) showed increasing expression from pHZ to LHZ in wild-type and can be defined as 'hypertrophy characteristic' genes.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis.

claim: Cluster IV genes were down-regulated in 13del LHZ.
source: Consistent with a change in the HC de-differentiation state in 13del, these genes were down-regulated in 13del LHZ.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis.

claim: The concomitant down-regulation of Cluster I stress response genes in 13del LHZ is consistent with the alleviation of the stress in the reprogrammed cells and an adapted state.
source: The concomitant down-regulation of Cluster I stress response genes in 13del LHZ is consistent with the alleviation of the stress in the reprogrammed cells and an adapted state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the clustering data.

claim: 227 genes were commonly changed in the microarray dataset compared with published data from two other MCDS mouse models.
source: We further compared our microarray dataset with the published data (Cameron et al., 2011) from another 2 MCDS mouse models, expressing a Col10a1 p.N617K mutation or an ER stress-inducing form of thyroglobulin (Tgcog) (Cameron et al., 2011). Overall, the gene expression changes detected in all datasets shared some degree of similarity, and 227 genes were commonly changed, showing the activation of ER stress signaling in the MCDS chondrocytes, up-regulation of genes such as Fgf21 and down-regulation of genes such as Ldb3.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published data.

claim: 473 genes were specifically changed in 13del.
source: Differences were also found, and 473 genes were specifically changed in 13del, such as Apoa4 (up-regulated) and Atp2a1 (down-regulated) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published data.

claim: Ontology and pathway analyses of Cluster I found enrichment of genes in the PERK pathway and IRE1-Xbp1S regulated ERAD, but not for ATF6 signaling.
source: By ontology and pathway analyses of Cluster I, we found enrichment of genes in the PERK pathway and IRE1-Xbp1S regulated ERAD, but not for ATF6 signaling (Figure 1D and E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Supplementary file 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by ontology and pathway analyses shown in figures.

claim: Activation of PERK signaling in 13del HC was demonstrated by up-regulation of p-eIF2α and its downstream components (Atf4, Atf3, Ddit3, Ero1l and Ppp1r15a).
source: Activation of PERK signaling in 13del HC was demonstrated by up-regulation of p-eIF2α and its downstream components (Atf4, Atf3, Ddit3, Ero1l and Ppp1r15a) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and C) which were validated by in-situ hybridization and immunostaining (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data and validated by in-situ hybridization and immunostaining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Motif enrichment analysis found that the binding motifs of CHOP and ATF4 were highly enriched in Cluster I, but not those for Xbp1S or ATF6.
source: Using Motif enrichment analysis, we found that the binding motifs of CHOP (encoded by Ddit3) and ATF4 were highly enriched in Cluster I, but not those for Xbp1S or ATF6 (Figure 1F and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ATF4 and CHOP ChIP-seq data showed significant over-representation of ATF4 and CHOP binding peaks associated with genes from Cluster I.
source: By interrogating ATF4 and CHOP ChIP-seq data (Han et al., 2013), we found significant over-representation of ATF4 (odds ratio = 2.87, p<0.0001) and CHOP (odds ratio = 4.33, p<0.0001) binding peaks associated with the genes from Cluster I but not for the other clusters (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published ChIP-seq data.

claim: Cluster I genes are most likely to be directly regulated by UPR-associated transcription factors.
source: Cluster I genes are therefore most likely to be directly regulated by UPR-associated transcription factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on motif enrichment and ChIP-seq analyses.

claim: Inactivation of Xbp1 in HCs did not alter the severity of dwarfism in an MCDS mouse model.
source: Together, these data suggest a more prominent contribution of the PERK-p-eIF2 signaling pathway than that of Xbp1S, which is consistent with another MCDS mouse model study that found inactivation of Xbp1 in HCs did not alter the severity of dwarfism (Cameron et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Overexpression of Xbp1S specifically in HCs did not affect the growth plate.
source: To test this notion, we ectopically expressed Xbp1S in HCs in transgenic mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A). Overexpression of Xbp1S specifically in HCs did not affect the growth plate (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data from transgenic mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: ATF4 is required for chondrocyte differentiation through direct activation of Ihh.
source: Apart from its role in the stress response, ATF4 is also required for chondrocyte differentiation through direct activation of Ihh (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In the E14.5-E17.5 fetal growth plate, ATF4 is expressed in differentiating chondrocytes, with the highest expression in pHCs.
source: In the E14.5-E17.5 fetal growth plate, ATF4 is expressed in differentiating chondrocytes, with the highest expression in pHCs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ATF4 expression in HCs progressively decreases after birth and by p10 levels are especially lowered in the LHZ.
source: ATF4 expression in HCs progressively decreases after birth and by p10 levels are especially lowered in the LHZ (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: C10-Atf4 transgenic mice were generated carrying a Col10-Bac-Atf4-IRES-Egfp transgene in which ATF4 expression was driven by the HC-specific promoter of Col10a1.
source: To assess the impact of ATF4 overexpression in HCs in the absence of ER stress, we generated a transgenic mouse model carrying a Col10-Bac-Atf4-IRES-Egfp transgene (hereafter referred to as C10-Atf4) (Figure 2B), in which ATF4 expression was driven by the highly HC-specific promoter of Col10a1 (Leung et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by Figure 2B.

claim: HC-specific expression of the C10-Atf4 transgene was confirmed in developing growth plates from fetal (E15.5) to adult (p20) stages.
source: We confirmed HC-specific expression of the C10-Atf4 transgene in the developing growth plates from fetal (E15.5) to adult (p20) stages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Adult C10-Atf4 transgenic mice were dwarfs, being approximately 20% shorter than wild-type littermates.
source: Similar to 13del mice, adult C10-Atf4 transgenic mice were dwarfs, being approximately 20% shorter than wild-type littermates (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by radiographic and body length measurements shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Histological analyses revealed growth plate abnormality in both the appendicular and axial skeleton of C10-Atf4 mice.
source: Histological analyses revealed growth plate abnormality in both the appendicular and axial skeleton. These defects are illustrated by the greater than three-fold expansion of the HZ of the tibia and vertebrae of C10-Atf4 mice (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The HZ expansion is more severe in C10-Atf4 mice (threefold of WT) than that in 13del (2.5-fold of WT).
source: Interestingly, the HZ expansion is more severe in C10-Atf4 mice (threefold of WT) than that in 13del (2.5-fold of WT), which is paralleling to the expression level of ATF4.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of histological measurements.

claim: Cell viability was not affected in C10-Atf4 mice.
source: Although forced expression of ATF4 in fibroblasts was reported to decrease survival (Han et al., 2013), cell viability was not affected in C10-Atf4 mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Overexpression of ATF4 in HCs in the absence of ER stress did not induce transcription of the UPR-associated genes Hspa5 and Ddit3.
source: Importantly, overexpression of ATF4 in HCs in the absence of ER stress did not induce transcription of the UPR-associated genes Hspa5 and Ddit3 (Figure 2F), although Atf3 was slightly upregulated (Han et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by in-situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Activation of ATF4 alone, in the absence of the ER stress response, is sufficient to alter HC differentiation, disturb endochondral ossification and cause skeletal abnormalities similar to those observed in 13del mice.
source: Therefore, activation of ATF4 alone, in the absence of the ER stress response, is sufficient to alter HC differentiation, disturb endochondral ossification and cause skeletal abnormalities similar to those observed in 13del mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the C10-Atf4 mouse phenotype data.

claim: In C10-Atf4 HCs, constitutive ATF4 activation down-regulated the expression of Col10a1 and led to persistent expression of prehypertrophic chondrocyte marker genes Sox9, Col2a1, Ppr and Ihh in the HZ.
source: In C10-Atf4 HCs, constitutive ATF4 activation down-regulated the expression of Col10a1 and led to persistent expression of prehypertrophic chondrocyte marker genes Sox9, Col2a1, Ppr and Ihh in the HZ (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by in-situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: BrdU-labeled HCs were not detectable in the C10-Atf4 HZ after 2 hr.
source: However, BrdU-labeled HCs were not detectable in the C10-Atf4 HZ after 2 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), suggesting C10-Atf4 HCs did not appear to have progressed through the G1/S checkpoint.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: ATF4 ChIP-Seq data showed ATF4 binding peaks in the regulatory regions of Sox9, Sox5, Sox6, Runx2, Gli2 and Gli3.
source: We searched the published ER stress-associated ATF4 ChIP-Seq data (Han et al., 2013) for binding peaks in crucial chondrogenic transcription factor genes, including members of SOX, RUNX, MEF2, GLI and FOXA families. We found ATF4 binding peaks in the regulatory regions of Sox9, Sox5, Sox6, Runx2, Gli2 and Gli3.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published ChIP-Seq data.

claim: Only the Sox genes were up-regulated in 13del middle and lower zones, but not Gli2 or Gli3.
source: Amongst these, only the Sox genes were up-regulated in 13del middle and lower zones, but not Gli2 or Gli3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that the Sox family could be the targets of ATF4.
evidence: This is supported by microarray and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Overexpression of Sox9 in HCs resulted in an expansion of HZ and impaired terminal differentiation of HCs.
source: Notably, overexpression of Sox9 in HCs resulted in an expansion of HZ and impaired terminal differentiation of HCs, similar to the phenotypes observed in C10-Atf4 mice (Hattori et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Two putative C/EBP-ATF4 motifs, named A1 and A2, were identified in the ATF4-binding peak in the Sox9 promoter region.
source: We identified two putative C/EBP-ATF4 motifs, named A1 and A2, in the ATF4-binding peak in the Sox9 promoter region.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Sox9 promoter sequence.

claim: ATF4 could transactivate luciferase reporters controlled by the Sox9 promoter in transfection assays in ATDC5 chondrocyte cells.
source: By transfection assays in ATDC5 chondrocyte cells, we found ATF4 could transactivate luciferase reporters controlled by the Sox9 promoter (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutation of A1 and A2 respectively reduced or abolished ATF4 activation of the Sox9 reporters.
source: Mutation of A1 and A2 respectively reduced or abolished ATF4 activation of the Sox9 reporters (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Anti-ATF4 ChIP-PCR assays demonstrated that ATF4 binds directly to the putative motif region on the Sox9 promoter in vivo.
source: Anti-ATF4 ChIP-PCR assays, using nuclear extracts from E15.5 wild-type and C10-Atf4 limbs, demonstrated that ATF4 binds directly to the putative motif region on the Sox9 promoter in vivo (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Conditional inactivation of Sox9 in C10-Atf4 HC markedly reduced the expansion of HZ.
source: We next assessed the contribution of ATF4 activation of Sox9 in reverting HC differentiation by conditionally inactivating Sox9 in C10-Atf4 HC, using HC-specific Col10a1-Cre (Yang et al., 2014) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). In the absence of Sox9, the expansion of HZ in C10-Atf4 mice was markedly reduced, and there were fewer cells expressing Col2a1 in the HZ (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by histological and quantitative data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Conditional inactivation of Sox9 in 13del mice decreased expression of Col2a1 and Ppr in HC, and the HZ expansion was considerably shortened.
source: Moreover, conditional inactivation of Sox9 in 13del mice decreased expression of Col2a1 and Ppr in HC, and the HZ expansion was considerably shortened (Figure 4D–F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by histological and quantitative data shown in Figure 4D–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Deletion of Sox9 in wild-type HCs did not affect chondrocyte hypertrophy.
source: Deletion of Sox9 in wild-type HCs did not affect chondrocyte hypertrophy (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ER stress-induced overexpression of ATF4 reverts differentiation in 13del HC by direct activation of Sox9 in HCs, thereby perturbing chondrocyte hypertrophy.
source: Collectively, these data suggest ER stress-induced overexpression of ATF4 reverts differentiation in 13del HC by direct activation of Sox9 in HCs, thereby perturbing chondrocyte hypertrophy.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic rescue experiments.

claim: CHOP is preferentially expressed in the PERK signaling pathway, downstream of p-eIF2α and ATF4.
source: CHOP is another prominent transcription factor that was active in 13del HCs, revealed by bioinformatics analysis. It is preferentially expressed in the PERK signaling pathway, downstream of p-eIF2α and ATF4, which regulates protein synthesis via the PPP1R15A negative feedback loop and restores protein synthesis and induces oxidative stress via Ero1l (Han et al., 2013; Marciniak et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Overexpression of CHOP in the bone microenvironment in transgenic mice has been reported to impair osteoblastic function leading to osteopenia.
source: Apart from that, overexpression of CHOP in the bone microenvironment in transgenic mice has been reported to impair osteoblastic function leading to osteopenia (Pereira et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: CHOP null mice show retarded bone formation.
source: while CHOP null mice show retarded bone formation (Pereira et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: CHOP has context- and cell-type specific roles as an adaptive and pro-survival factor in several diseases.
source: Although CHOP is widely considered as a pro-apoptotic factor, it has context- and cell-type specific roles as an adaptive and pro-survival factor in several diseases (Pennuto et al., 2008; Southwood et al., 2002; Lu et al., 2014; Moreno et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ablating CHOP in 13del mice exacerbated the skeletal defects and growth plate phenotype.
source: We found ablating CHOP encoding gene Ddit3 in 13del mice exacerbated the skeletal defects and growth plate phenotype. The 13del;Ddit3-/- mice displayed further tibial shortening (Figure 5A and B) with more significant (~20%) HZ expansion (Figure 5C and D), and increased the number of chondrocytes expressing immature chondrogenic markers SOX9, Col2a1 and Ppr in the HZ (Figure 5C and E).
evidence: This is supported by histological and quantitative data shown in Figure 5A–E.

claim: There was increased apoptosis in 13del;Ddit3-/- HC.
source: Strikingly, in contrast to 13del, there was increased apoptosis in 13del;Ddit3-/- HC, consistent with a pro-survival role for CHOP (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: Transcriptome analyses of fractionated 13del;Ddit3-/- growth plates revealed upregulation of molecular chaperones (Hspa5, Dnajb9, Dnajb11 and Canx) and ER stress sensors (Xbp1 and Atf4) in the MHZ and LHZ.
source: Our transcriptome analyses of fractionated 13del;Ddit3-/- growth plates revealed upregulation of molecular chaperones (Hspa5, Dnajb9, Dnajb11 and Canx) and ER stress sensors (Xbp1 and Atf4) in the MHZ and LHZ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In 13del;Ddit3-/- mice, the PERK signaling pathway was enfeebled, reflected by marked (>3.5 fold) down-regulation of CHOP targets Atf3, Ppp1r15a and Ero1l.
source: In contrast to the elevated stress level, the PERK signaling pathway was enfeebled, reflected by marked (>3.5 fold) down-regulation of CHOP targets Atf3, Ppp1r15a and Ero1l, indicating the phenotype severity reflected by aberrant cell differentiation is probably independent of those downstream factors.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data.

claim: CHOP aids in the cell adaptation to stress and mediates survival in 13del HC.
source: Therefore, CHOP aids in the cell adaptation to stress and mediates survival in13del HC, and it is important to identify pro-survival/anti apoptotic factor(s) downstream of CHOP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the 13del;Ddit3-/- phenotype data.

claim: Fgf21 was the most upregulated gene in 13del HCs.
source: CHOP acts, not only downstream of ATF4 but also as its interacting partner in modulating ER stress targets (Han et al., 2013). To elucidate the pro-survival role of the PERK signaling pathway in 13del HC, we searched for target genes of CHOP and ATF4 in Cluster I (Supplementary file 6). We found Fgf21, a reported target of ATF4 (65), was the most upregulated gene in 13del HCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1), which was confirmed by in-situ hybridization and immunoblotting (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray, in-situ hybridization, and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Fgf21 has been reported to be similarly activated in ER-stressed chondrocytes.
source: Fgf21 has been reported to be similarly activated in ER-stressed chondrocytes (Cameron et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: FGF21 is a hormone with roles in glucose and lipid metabolism.
source: FGF21 is a hormone with roles in glucose and lipid metabolism (Kharitonenkov et al., 2005)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: FGF21 plays a survival role in response to diverse stressful conditions, such as amino acid deprivation, mitochondrial stress and ER stress-associated diseases.
source: and plays a survival role in response to diverse stressful conditions, such as amino acid deprivation, mitochondrial stress and ER stress-associated diseases such as diabetes, cardiovascular diseases (reviewed in [Gómez-Sámano et al., 2017; Kim and Lee, 2015; Salminen et al., 2017]).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Fgf21 expression was effectively turned on (>100 fold increased expression) in response to treatment with the ER stress inducer tunicamycin in fibroblasts (NIH3T3 and MEF cells) and ATDC5 cells.
source: We found Fgf21 expression was effectively turned on (>100 fold increased expression) in response to treatment with the ER stress inducer tunicamycin in fibroblasts (NIH3T3 and MEF cells) and ATDC5 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Deleting or mutating the ATF4 binding motif in the Fgf21 promoter abolished the activation induced by ER stress in transactivation assays.
source: We next tested the functional relevance of a reported C/EBP-ATF4 binding motif in the Fgf21 promoter (Han et al., 2013) that coincided with an ATF4 peak. By transactivation assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), we found deleting (pFgf21-Luc3 and pFgf21-Luc4) or mutating (pFgf21-M1 and pFgf21-M3) the ATF4 binding motif abolished the activation induced by ER stress.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Fgf21 was not induced in C10-Atf4 mice.
source: However, Fgf21 was not induced in C10-Atf4 mice (Figure 6B), suggesting ATF4 is necessary but not sufficient for Fgf21 induction.
evidence: This is supported by in-situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Both ATF4 and CHOP bind to the ATF4 motif-containing peak region in the Fgf21 promoter in cells under ER stress.
source: The need for another factor is supported by the ChIP assays where we found both ATF4 and CHOP bind to the ATF4 motif-containing peak region in the cells under ER stress (Figure 6C), even though no CHOP binding peak was detected in the Fgf21 promoter.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Expression of Fgf21 was down-regulated by approximately 40% in 13del;Ddit3-/- HC despite the upregulation of Atf4.
source: Expression of Fgf21 was down-regulated by approximately 40% in 13del;Ddit3-/- HC despite the upregulation of Atf4 (Figure 6D), consistent with the requirement of ATF4-CHOP cooperation for Fgf21 induction under ER stress.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Fgf21 null mice have normal growth plates and HC viability.
source: We assessed whether FGF21 had a survival role in 13del HC by genetically ablating the gene (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). Fgf21 null mice have normal growth plates and HC viability (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by histological and TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The HZ expansion in 13del;Fgf21-/- mice was comparable to that of 13del mice, and the reverted differentiation process was not affected.
source: The HZ expansion in 13del;Fgf21-/- mice was comparable to that of 13del mice, and the reverted differentiation process was not affected (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by histological and quantitative data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: There was increased apoptosis in the HZ of Fgf21-deficient 13del mice, and this protective effect of FGF21 is dosage dependent.
source: However, we found increased apoptosis in the HZ of Fgf21-deficient 13del mice, and this protective effect of FGF21 is dosage dependent (Figure 7Aand B).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: In 13del;Col10a1EGFP/13 del;Fgf21-/- chimeras, more 13del;Fgf21-/- HCs (non-EGFP+ HC population) underwent apoptosis, than the 13del; Col10a1Egfp HCs (GFP+ HC population).
source: Similarly as found with 13del;Fgf21-/- compound mutants, in 13del;Col10a1EGFP/13 del;Fgf21-/- chimeras, more 13del;Fgf21-/- HCs (non-EGFP+ HC population) underwent apoptosis, than the 13del; Col10a1Egfp HCs (GFP+ HC population) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data in chimeras shown in Figure 7D.

claim: There was a positive correlation between the contribution of13del;Col10a1Egfp HCs and the number of surviving cells in the HZ.
source: Moreover, there was a positive correlation between the contribution of13del;Col10a1Egfp HCs and the number of surviving cells in the HZ (Figure 7E), consistent with a protective role for FGF21 in the ER-stressed 13del HCs.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: 13del;Fgf21-/- HCs adjacent to 13del;Col10a1Egfp HCs expressing Fgf21 still underwent apoptosis.
source: Furthermore, we found that 13del;Fgf21-/- HCs adjacent to 13del;Col10a1Egfp HCs expressing Fgf21 still underwent apoptosis (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: FGF21 protects HCs from apoptosis cell autonomously.
source: This inability of 13del;Col10a1Egfp to rescue 13del;Fgf21-/- HCs suggests that FGF21 protects HCs from apoptosis, cell autonomously.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the chimera experiments.

claim: PERK phosphorylation of eIF2α is the critical upstream controlling point that triggers the p-eIF2α/ATF4/CHOP signaling pathway.
source: Upon ER stress, PERK phosphorylation of eIF2α is the critical upstream controlling point that triggers the p-eIF2α/ATF4/CHOP signaling pathway (Pakos‐-Zebrucka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ISRIB is a small molecule that is a potent ISR signaling inhibitor, rendering cells insensitive to eIF2α phosphorylation by targeting the interaction between eIF2 and eIF2B.
source: Recently, a small molecule, Integrated Stress Response InhiBitor (ISRIB) has been reported to be a potent ISR signaling inhibitor, rendering cells insensitive to eIF2α phosphorylation by targeting the interaction between eIF2 and eIF2B, and its activity is independent of eIF2a phosphorylation (Sekine et al., 2015; Sidrauski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ISRIB shows acceptable pharmacokinetic properties and no overall toxicity in mice.
source: ISRIB shows acceptable pharmacokinetic properties and no overall toxicity in mice and has been reported to show significant neurotrophic effects in mice (Sekine et al., 2015; Di Prisco et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In wild-type mice, ISRIB had no adverse effects on weight gain or body growth.
source: We tested the potential of ISRIB to modify the chondrodysplasia phenotype by treating 13del and wild-type littermates with ISRIB (2.5 mg/kg) or vehicle twice daily by intraperitoneal injection from E13.5 (onset of expression of 13del) to postnatal day 20 (p20) (Figure 8A). In wild-type mice, ISRIB had no adverse effects on weight gain or body growth (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by body weight and length measurements shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: ISRIB markedly reduced the dwarfism of 13del mice from newborn to juvenile stages.
source: However, ISRIB markedly reduced the dwarfism of 13del mice from newborn to juvenile stages comparing to control group (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by body length measurements shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Treatment with ISRIB ameliorated the skeletal deformities at p20 in 13del mice.
source: Radiographic analyses revealed treatment with ISRIB ameliorated the skeletal deformities at p20 (Figure 8B and C), including the length of tibia/femur and spine; tibia bowing (genu varum: the angle between proximal head and distal head of tibia); pelvic bone orientation (the angle between ilium and pubis), and coxa vara (narrowed angle between the proximal head and the shaft of the femur) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by radiographic analyses shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: The HZ expansion in the limb growth plates of ISRIB-treated 13del mice was significantly reduced.
source: We found the HZ expansion in the limb growth plates of ISRIB-treated 13del mice was significantly reduced, and the numbers of SOX9+, Col2a1+ and Ppr+ cells in the HZs at p10 and p20 were diminished (Figure 8D–G).
evidence: This is supported by histological and quantitative data shown in Figure 8D–G.

claim: ISRIB treatment in 13del mice reduced the deformities in other growth plates such as in the axial skeleton.
source: ISRIB treatment in 13del mice also reduced the deformities in other growth plates such as in the axial skeleton, with reduced HZ expansion and decreased the number of Sox9+ and Col2a1+ premature cells in tail intervertebral disc growth plates (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Postnatal treatment of ISRIB in 13del MCDS ameliorated the dwarfism and skeletal deformities in a dosage-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, the effectiveness of postnatal treatment of ISRIB in 13del MCDS was estimated by treating 13del and wild-type littermates with ISRIB (2.5 mg/kg or 5 mg/kg) or vehicle twice daily by intraperitoneal injection from newborn (p0) to 4-week stages (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A). Similarly, ISRIB ameliorated the dwarfism of 13del mice from newborn to 4-week stages in a dosage-dependent manner (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B), and ameliorated the skeletal deformities (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C and D)
evidence: This is supported by body length and radiographic data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3B–D.

claim: The expression of p-eIF2α was not affected in ISRIB-treated 13del HCs.
source: Consistent with the previous study (Sidrauski et al., 2013) that the activity of ISRIB is independent of eIF2α phosphorylation (Sekine et al., 2015; Sidrauski et al., 2015), the expression of p-eIF2α was not affected in ISRIB-treated 13del HCs (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: ISRIB evidently inhibited the preferential translation of ATF4 in ER-stressed 13del HCs.
source: Given the fact that translational regulation of ATF4 by p-eIF2α is central to the activation of PERK signaling, the protein expression level of ATF4 in p10 vehicle-treated WT, vehicle- and ISRIB-treated 13del HCs were examined via immunoblotting. As expected, ISRIB evidently inhibited the preferential translation of ATF4 in ER-stressed 13del HCs (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: ISRIB treatment significantly downregulated the mRNA expression level of Atf3 and Ddit3 in 13del HCs.
source: The proximal growth plates from above mentioned groups of mice were further fractionated into sub-populations (PC, pHC, UHC, MHC, and LHC), and the transcriptional expression levels of major components of p-eIF2α signaling (Atf4, Atf3, Ddit3 and Fgf21), Xbp1S and Hspa5 (Bip) were examined by qRT-PCR. Consistently, ISRIB treatment significantly downregulated the mRNA expression level of Atf3 and Ddit3 in 13del HCs, indicating the downstream signaling cascade of ATF4 were inhibited (Figure 9C), although the expression level of Atf4 was not affected.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The expression level of total Xbp1 (Xbp1T) and spliced Xbp1 (Xbp1S) in ISRIB-treated 13del HCs was comparable to vehicle-treated HCs.
source: On the other hand, the expression level of total Xbp1 (Xbp1T) and spliced Xbp1 (Xbp1S) in ISRIB-treated 13del HCs was comparable to vehicle-treated HCs, indicating IRE1/Xbp1 signaling was barely affected and confirmed the selectivity of ISRIB action (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The effects of ISRIB on ameliorating 13del MCDS phenotype is Xbp1S-independent.
source: Thus, the effects of ISRIB on ameliorating 13del MCDS phenotype is Xbp1S-independent, and it further supports the redundancy of IRE1/Xbp1 signaling in the pathogenesis of MCDS (Cameron et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the qRT-PCR data and supported by citation.

claim: The transcriptional and translational expression levels of ER chaperone BiP were relatively attenuated in ISRIB-treated 13del HCs.
source: Also, the transcriptional and translational expression levels of ER chaperone BiP(encoded by Hspa5) were relatively attenuated in ISRIB-treated 13del HCs (Figure 9B and C), consistent with previous studies showing that PERK-p-eIF2α signaling is required for the activation of BiP upon ER stress (Harding et al., 2000; Scheuner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 9B and C, and citations.

claim: The 13DEL mutant protein was intracellularly accumulated in ISRIB-treated 13del HCs.
source: Immunostaining with a 13DEL-specific antibody revealed the 13DEL mutant protein were intracellularly accumulated in ISRIB-treated 13del HCs (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C), indicating the production and/or degradation of the mutant protein was not affected.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Inhibition of p-eIF2α signaling by ISRIB at indicated dosage did not induce apoptosis in 13del HCs.
source: Interestingly, inhibition of p-eIF2α signaling by ISRIB at indicated dosage did not induce apoptosis (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D) in 13del HCs, with a lowered expression level of ATF4, CHOP and FGF21.
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The effects of ISRIB on ameliorating 13del MCDS phenotype depends explicitly on downregulating p-eIF2α modulated ATF4 induction and its downstream target SOX9.
source: Thus, the effects of ISRIB on ameliorating 13del MCDS phenotype depends explicitly on downregulating p-eIF2α modulated ATF4 induction and its downstream target SOX9.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ISRIB treatment data.
